observations.statement: The excerpt defines authoritative threshold and exhaustion transitions, default percentage thresholds, signal-authority precedence, and preservation of provider-named quota windows.
Soft pressure escalates from informational to approaching-threshold on repetition, while reset expiry moves an account into revalidation instead of directly restoring readiness.
Cooldown and retry budget are first-class account state, and an authoritative cooldown hard-blocks routing until post-expiry revalidation.
Default auto-switching spans assistant, interviewer, builder, overseer, and node-worker actors, with requested/effective identity fields and durable switch and pressure history.
The excerpt establishes PM-owned account roots and deny-by-default sharing classes while permitting explicitly modeled copy, symlink, generated, and provider-API projections.
The GUI contract includes a prelaunch Effective Runtime prediction, lifecycle labels, account removal choices, reassignment, and a per-provider default-account invariant.

candidate_findings.title: Failover lacks an operation-level retry boundary
candidate_findings.claim: The excerpt enables default auto-switching and makes retry budget first-class, but it does not specify whether an already-started provider operation is abandoned, resumed, replayed on another account, or retried only for a later request. It also supplies no idempotency boundary or duplicate-side-effect rule for builders and node workers.
candidate_findings.why_it_matters: A refusal or disconnect after partial output or tool activity can either lose work or replay side effects. Implementations could make incompatible choices while all appearing to satisfy the account-switch policy.

candidate_findings.title: Soft-pressure escalation has no deterministic oracle
candidate_findings.claim: The terms `repeated soft signals` and `repeated plan-pressure signals` have no count, time window, deduplication key, decay rule, or reset condition in the excerpt.
candidate_findings.why_it_matters: Equivalent telemetry streams can produce different pressure states and switching behavior across implementations, and no bounded conformance test can determine when escalation is correct.

candidate_findings.title: Multiple quota windows lack an aggregation policy
candidate_findings.claim: The excerpt preserves named windows such as `fiveHour` and `weekly` and defines percentage thresholds, but it does not say which window controls eligibility when windows disagree, how missing counters are handled, or how absolute and percentage limits are normalized.
candidate_findings.why_it_matters: One window can be exhausted while another is healthy. Without an aggregation rule, identical account telemetry can yield conflicting routing and recovery decisions.

candidate_findings.title: Role-aware routing lacks an account-authorization model
candidate_findings.claim: `execution_role` and role-aware selection are recorded, but the excerpt defines no role-to-account allowlist, credential-use scope, tenant boundary, or authorization decision explaining which assistant, builder, overseer, or node worker may use a particular account.
candidate_findings.why_it_matters: Default auto-switching could move a worker onto an account whose billing, organization, data policy, or credentials it is not authorized to use.

candidate_findings.title: Concurrent health and switch updates have no ordering rule
candidate_findings.claim: Every provider-using interaction may update account health, all provider-using actor classes can auto-switch, and switch history is durable, but the excerpt gives no serialization, versioning, stale-write rejection, reservation, or conflict-resolution rule for concurrent updates.
candidate_findings.why_it_matters: Parallel workers can simultaneously select nominal capacity, oversubscribe an account, overwrite newer health, or oscillate between accounts despite retry budgets.

candidate_findings.title: Filesystem isolation lacks hostile-path enforcement
candidate_findings.claim: The excerpt defines account roots, allows selective symlink sharing, and declares deny classes, but it does not define canonical-path containment, symlink traversal checks, file ownership and permission requirements, race-safe projection, or validation that projected content cannot escape an account root.
candidate_findings.why_it_matters: A malicious or stale symlink and permissive filesystem metadata can bypass logical deny classes and leak auth state, histories, tokens, trust state, or caches between account profiles.

candidate_findings.title: Overlapping state vocabularies have no crosswalk or precedence
candidate_findings.negative_space_dimension: states, transitions, and misleading GUI truth
candidate_findings.claim: Pressure states, cooldown and hard-block state, provider-specific auth states, GUI lifecycle labels, and the registration `status` enum coexist without a closed mapping or precedence rule for simultaneous conditions.
candidate_findings.why_it_matters: An account can be logged in, disabled, cooling down, validation-failed, and registration-active at once. Without precedence, the GUI label, routing eligibility, remediation action, and persisted status can contradict one another.

candidate_findings.title: Pick-best ordering is under-specified
candidate_findings.claim: The excerpt uses `healthy enough`, `highest-ranked viable auth surface`, and `strongest available account-health signals` without closing the viable-auth-surface ranking, a same-priority tie-breaker, or the health cutoff used for stickiness.
candidate_findings.why_it_matters: Schedulers can choose different effective accounts from the same candidate set, making routing tests nondeterministic and undermining the prelaunch runtime prediction.

candidate_findings.title: Account removal and archival are not transactional
candidate_findings.claim: Removal is required to reassign threads and defaults, and archival captures PM-managed artifacts first, but the excerpt does not define behavior for in-flight runs, partial archive failure, reassignment failure, rollback, archive retention or encryption, or cleanup of credentials held outside the named data stores.
candidate_findings.why_it_matters: A failed multi-step removal can orphan references, leave a removed identity active in a run, retain sensitive artifacts unexpectedly, or delete the account record while leaving usable credentials behind.

candidate_findings.title: The default-account invariant has no zero or ineligible state
candidate_findings.claim: Each provider must have exactly one default account, yet providers can have no eligible backup, providers can be disabled without deleting rows, and accounts can be removed. The excerpt does not state how the invariant is represented or repaired when the last account is removed or the default becomes disabled, invalid, blocked, or unready.
candidate_findings.why_it_matters: Implementations may retain an unusable default, invent a replacement, violate the exactly-one invariant, or silently route through a non-default account.

candidate_findings.title: Revalidation can remain pending indefinitely
candidate_findings.claim: Reset or cooldown expiry moves an account to validation and successful revalidation is required before reuse, but the excerpt defines no probe scheduling, timeout, backoff, retry ceiling, offline behavior, or terminal state when revalidation cannot complete.
candidate_findings.why_it_matters: Recovered capacity can remain unusable forever, or implementations can probe indefinitely and create load, without a common operational or user-remediation outcome.

candidate_findings.title: Effective Runtime prediction lacks freshness and reconciliation semantics
candidate_findings.claim: The inspector predicts a likely requested/effective runtime and rows show a last-validation timestamp, while the final run record preserves requested/effective entries. The excerpt does not require the prediction to expose its data age, source authority, uncertainty, or a reconciliation state when launch-time selection differs.
candidate_findings.why_it_matters: Users can interpret a stale prediction as a commitment and miss that billing identity, account, capabilities, or provider changed at launch.

candidate_findings.title: Routing authority precedence is incomplete
candidate_findings.claim: The excerpt defines hard no-fallback constraints, manual set-active/preferred controls, `required` account binding, role-aware policy, provider enablement, and a provider default, but it does not provide a total precedence order among those authorities.
candidate_findings.why_it_matters: A scheduler cannot deterministically resolve conflicts such as a manual preferred account versus a run-required account, a provider default versus role policy, or a required account that is disabled or invalid.

explicit_non_gaps.statement: Authoritative remaining counters have explicit threshold and exhaustion defaults, and runtime token statistics alone are prohibited from creating a hard block or exhausted state.
The excerpt explicitly enumerates conditions under which auto-switching must not occur.
Expiry of a reset or cooldown does not blindly restore readiness; successful revalidation is required before routing resumes.
Manual override remains distinguishable from the default model and still records requested identity, effective identity, and switch reason.
Sensitive provider-generated and account-bearing state is explicitly denied from cross-account sharing by default, and deny classes win over sharing classes.
The GUI lifecycle explicitly distinguishes logged-in state from ready state and requires provider-specific degraded-state fidelity.
Family-pool selection requires effective capability checks and preserves requested and effective provider entries with explicit Antigravity/Gemini Direct transition disclosure.
Account removal distinguishes PM-only removal from removal with archival and explicitly requires reassignment of thread and default references.

exact_evidence_refs.excerpt:
For authoritative remaining counters, PM drives `threshold_reached` at `<= configured switch threshold` and drives `exhausted` at `0 remaining` or explicit provider exhaustion. Provider `/accounts` may override these defaults, but the scheduler must not leave the state transition undefined when authoritative remaining quota is available.
Default threshold-aware policy uses warning threshold `20% remaining` and default auto-switch threshold `10% remaining` unless provider/account overrides say otherwise. Per-account observed `/provider-reported` effective limits outrank generic provider-doc defaults, while provider docs preserve documented/default expectations when effective observed state differs. Providers with named windows preserve provider window keys such as `fiveHour` and `weekly`, and authoritative Gemini quota or `/reset` data outranks runtime token stats when deciding whether to recover back to a primary account. For coding-plan direct providers, official `/reset` and `/remains` endpoints and documented windows are authoritative defaults until observed account-specific divergence wins. Runtime token stats alone can influence pressure, but they must not become a `hard_block` or exhausted state without explicit quota, refusal, cooldown, or equivalent authoritative evidence.

For softer provider/runtime evidence, one weak signal is informational, repeated soft signals move the account/profile to `approaching_threshold`, and explicit refusal, cooldown, or lockout moves it to `exhausted` or a blocked state.
PM must not auto-switch purely on one soft `plan-warning`; repeated `plan-pressure` signals can move the account/profile to `approaching_threshold` before stronger refusal or cooldown evidence marks exhaustion.
When a known provider `reset_at` passes, PM moves the affected account/profile to `validating` or `eligible_pending_recheck` rather than blindly marking it `ready`.

Do NOT auto-switch when:
- no eligible backup account exists
- policy forbids it
- provider capability does not support it
- a hard requested constraint forbids fallback
- the current account is in `needs_configuration` / `validation_required` / invalid-credential state and policy requires explicit user recovery first

Cooldown / retry-budget rules:
- cooldown is first-class provider/account state
- retry budget is first-class provider/account state
- on exhaustion or severe rate limit, mark cooldown and avoid bouncing back immediately
- retry budget prevents thrashing the same account repeatedly
- an authoritative cooldown with `cooldown_until` sets `hard_block=true` and state `cooldown` until revalidation after expiry

- manual `set active` / preferred account exists as an override/debug control
- manual control does not redefine the default operating model
- manual control still records requested vs effective account identity and switch reason

- The `clausona` pattern is allowed only as evidence for selective Claude Code sharing: PM may share supported mutable assets by `symlink` when the account boundary remains explicit, while `.claude.json` and usually `projects/` stay isolated account-local state.

- Each selectable account-like unit gets a stable PM-owned child root under that provider base: direct-account-like roots use `.../accounts/<account_id>/` and the `/accounts/<account_id>/` path family, while CLI account roots use `.../accounts/<account_id>/root/`, with `/root/` as the runnable CLI home segment under `/accounts/`.

- Gemini account and runtime records use requested/effective storage vocabulary, including `requested_auth_mode` and `effective_*` snapshots for auth, `/capability`, billing/quota plane, project context, and usage source. Non-secret preferences can live in project/account settings; OAuth/API credentials stay out of redb and `/seglog`.

- Across all CLI-backed providers, `auth_state`, `history`, `mcp_oauth_tokens`, `extensions runtime state`, `project registry`, `temp chats`, `workspace_trust`, `runtime_cache`, `cooldown_residue`, and `telemetry_state` are denied from sharing by default. PM-managed overlays may be projected separately, but account-bearing state and residue from one profile must not leak into another account's runnable profile.
- Runtime sharing defaults allow PM-managed overlays for instructions, skills, selected `mcp_definitions`, and selected bridge config only when target-specific; auth_state, trust/workspace_trust, cooldown `/usage` state, transcripts `/history`, temp chats, provider-generated session DBs, sessions, state db, model cache, projects, plans, stats cache, and runtime caches remain account-local/provider-generated unless an owner contract explicitly promotes them.
- Provider account sharing policy records include `share_classes[]`, `deny_classes[]`, and `projection_mode = copy | symlink | generated | provider_api`; `deny_classes[]` wins for account-bearing state, and any `provider_api` projection must remain a provider adapter boundary rather than a filesystem sharing shortcut.

The multi-account contract applies across assistant, interviewer, builders, overseers, and node workers.

Rules:
- multi-account auto-switching is on by default for provider-using actors
- provider selection is provider-aware, account-aware, and role-aware
- same-provider accounts are not interchangeable
- manual set-active is an override/debug control rather than the main execution model

Required account-binding/runtime fields are:
- `requested_account_policy`
- `requested_account_id?`
- `requested_account_binding?`
- `effective_account_id?`
- `account_switch_reason?`
- `execution_role`

`requested_account_binding` is closed to:
- `none`
- `preferred`
- `required`

Rules:
- `requested_account_policy` alone is not enough to explain concrete account selection
- failed or blocked switch decisions remain historically material even when `effective_account_id` does not change
- durable switch and pressure history is persisted through `account_switch_event` and `account_pressure_episode`
- normalized pressure-state trigger tables include `nominal` as the healthy/available state for rows with capacity above threshold, no active cooldown, and no higher-confidence hard block.
- Authoritative account-specific `hard_block=true` or `hard_blocked` evidence makes that account ineligible for routing, even when provider docs say the reset window should have elapsed; PM must preserve the documented-vs-observed mismatch as diagnostic context and wait for successful revalidation before routing to that account again.

## 8. Usage and pick-best
- Usage/account pressure plugs into the shared usage model; do not create a parallel quota system for multi-account routing.
- Every provider-using interaction may update account health.
- Pick-best uses the strongest available account-health signals plus configured policy; it does not treat all signals as equally authoritative.
- Any Gemini `/quota/status` projection that only reports provider-level state is incomplete: Gemini family summaries must preserve the account-level state that produced the current usage, pressure, cooldown, and source-confidence labels.

Priority, GUI ordering, and stickiness rules:
- lower numeric priority wins (`1` before `2` before `3`)
- prefer the current effective account if it remains healthy enough
- otherwise choose the highest-priority eligible account inside the highest-ranked viable auth surface
- do not bounce immediately back to a recovered higher-priority account unless policy and health justify it
A persistent `Effective Runtime` inspector remains visible in the provider detail flow and predicts the likely requested/effective runtime before launch.

Family-pool guardrails: PM may only auto-select a unit when its effective capabilities satisfy the requested model/media/effort/tooling needs, including `/media/effort/tooling` capability checks. The run record must preserve the requested provider entry and effective provider entry explicitly, and PM must never silently route a request into retired Gemini CLI-only features. Antigravity and Gemini Direct requested/effective transitions require explicit disclosure.

Each row shows:
- label
- auth family or profile mode
- current state
- derived auth/configuration/availability state
- pressure/cooldown summary
- entitlement/billing secondary line when relevant
- last validation or health timestamp
- primary actions appropriate to the row type

Required states:
- `Logged out` / `Logged Out`
- `Logging in` / `Logging In`
- `Logged in`
- `Needs setup`
- `Validating`
- `Ready`
- `Auth expired`
- `Validation failed`
- `Logging out`
- `Disabled`

Rules:
- The account/profile GUI `/state-machine` must retain enough provider-specific state to render these labels plus provider-specific degraded states rather than collapsing them into one generic error chip.
- `Logged in` is not the same as `Ready`.
- setup-state labels MUST treat `Logged In` as distinct from `Ready`; a `Use API Key` path can save credentials but still requires auth/config/entitlement validation before the row reaches `Ready`, selected `/account/profile` readiness requires `/config/entitlement` validation for the active provider/account/profile type, and unresolved entitlement/billing context keeps direct-provider setup in a `partial-setup` / configuration state rather than treating auth alone as sufficient.
- Provider-specific entitlement or `/billing` resolution can keep an account in `Needs setup` after auth succeeds; PM must not collapse that state into `Ready`, `partial-setup`, or `Logging Out`.

Required flows:
- **Add account:** `Settings -> Providers -> [Provider] -> Add Account`.
- **Edit account:** allow `display_name` changes and credential rotation; rotating a credential MUST trigger the provider's re-auth or revalidation flow before the updated row returns to `Ready`.
- **Remove account/profile:** present a confirmation dialog with `Remove from PM only` and `Remove and archive PM-managed data` choices. Both choices remove the account/profile record and reassign any threads or defaults pointing at that account/profile; only the archive choice captures PM-managed artifacts first.
- **Default account:** each provider has exactly one default account. PM uses that default whenever no explicit account selection is made by policy, role, or manual override.

- Gemini auth states are richer than a binary logged-in flag. `oauth_logged_out`, `oauth_logged_in`, `oauth_needs_project_context`, `oauth_needs_configuration`, and `api_key_configured` are distinct setup/readiness states. `oauth_needs_configuration` may be account-scoped when the selected account lacks project, billing, trust, or credential context; provider-scoped setup state is allowed only when every account under that provider entry shares the same missing configuration.

- new account rows use the canonical schema `{ account_id: ulid, provider_id, display_name, auth_method, credential_ref, created_at, last_used_at, status }`.
- `status` closes to `active | expired | revoked | error`.
- provider-level `Enable/Disable Provider` changes future eligibility only and must not destroy account/profile rows or saved defaults.
